newsitem.title: USA: White House's Stiglitz says U.S. NAIRU has fallen.
newsitem.headline: White House's Stiglitz says U.S. NAIRU has fallen.

text.p: A top White House economic adviser on Friday said the point at which a low unemployment rate can trigger upward pressure on inflation has fallen and could decline even further in the future.
Referring to what economists call the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, or "NAIRU," Stiglitz said,

"Our own preliminary finding shows that the NAIRU has fallen by 1.5 percentage points since its peak in the early 1980s," Stiglitz, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, told a conference of the American Economic Association.
He cautioned, however, that uncertainty surrounding that estimate was "very large."
Stiglitz declined to give an estimate for the NAIRU.

However, he said the present inflation situation -- at a time when the unemployment rate is 5.1 percent, its lowest level in seven years -- is evidence of NAIRU that is below the 6.0 to 6.2 percent range that many economists had previously estimated.

The White House economist said new forces in the economy, such as demographic changes and the changing nature of the labor force due to the fact that a lower rate of unemployment has been accommodated for a period of time, will likely reduce the NAIRU further.
Earlier the Labor Department reported that the Consumer Price Index in August rose a slight 0.1 percent both overall and in the "core rate," which excludes food and energy prices.
While applauding the latest inflation news, Stiglitz downplayed concerns that wage pressures are picking up and that inflation could move higher in coming months.
"Not only have we not seen any actual inflation but there is some evidence that inflationary pressures are not as great as many fear," Stiglitz said.
"We have yet to see wages putting pressure on prices," he added.

Although he urged a continued experiment to see how low the NAIRU actually is, Stiglitz cited a policy of the Clinton administration about not commenting on Federal Reserve policies and stressed that none of his remarks were a comment on the central bank.
Stiglitz was the second key administration official this week to discuss in depth the view that the NAIRU had fallen.
In a speech earlier this week in Boston, Labor Secretary Robert Reich highlighted many of the same points.
